extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of WWII history, journalists interested in wartime censorship practices
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of the United States Office of Censorship's policies, code, and operational practices for censoring or restricting news and communications during World War II. Covers legal authority, the voluntary Code of Wartime Practices, media-specific restrictions (radio, print, film), secrecy rules (Manhattan Project/radar), and examples of failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 8985 — director's absolute discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: On December 19, 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8985, which established the Office of Censorship and conferred on its director the power to censor international communications in "his absolute discretion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order also set up a Censorship Policy Board to advise the director and authorized a Censorship Operating Board to bring together other agencies. By March 1942, military personnel working on joint censorship operations were moved into the Office of Censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary regulatory code adopted by the press
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency's implementation of censorship was done primarily through a voluntary regulatory code that was willingly adopted by the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price emphasized voluntary cooperation (motto: "Least said, soonest mended") and the principle "what does not concern the war does not concern censorship." Rather than having government officials review all items, newspapers and radio stations were to seek approval from relevant government agencies before discussing sensitive subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Wartime Practices — subjects requiring authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code of Wartime Practices set forth subjects that contained information of value to the enemy and which, therefore, should not be published or broadcast in the United States without authorization by a qualified government source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code was concise (seven pages for broadcasters, five for printed press) and supported by a 24-hour hotline to answer media questions about appropriate topics. Major news organizations and 1,600 accredited wartime correspondents pledged to adhere to the code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific sensitive subjects (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitive subjects explicitly included factory production figures, troop movements, damages to American forces, and weather reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories served as concrete examples of the kind of information that required prior authorization; journalists were instructed to seek clearance from the appropriate government source before publishing or broadcasting such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather reporting restrictions for broadcasters
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters were asked to use only specially approved Weather Bureau forecasts; from January 15, 1942 to October 12, 1943 broadcasters said nothing about rain, snow, fog, wind, air pressure, temperature, or sunshine unless it was approved by the Weather Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions were later added for emergency bulletins (after the Memphis tornado). The code considered weather so sensitive it briefly contemplated banning broadcasting outdoor sports, but ultimately allowed sports coverage for morale reasons. Examples include reprimanding Eleanor Roosevelt for describing weather in a column and praising an announcer who avoided saying "fog."

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on audience-participation and "man on the street" programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio stations had to discontinue programs with audience participation and man on the street interviews because of the risk that an enemy agent might use the microphone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations cooperated despite losing advertising revenue; Price estimated some program cancellations cost stations "tens of millions of dollars," though increased war advertising helped compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of potentially encoded transmissions (ads/requests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost-and-found advertisements ended and All Request programs were asked to avoid complying with specific times for music requests to prevent encoded transmission of secret data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures aimed to eliminate routine public features that could be repurposed to send covert signals to enemy agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on reporting presidential movements
rubrics_metrics.description: The code specifically restricted information on "movements of the President of the United States." Price reported directly to the President, effectively giving Roosevelt control over press reports about his travel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice included limiting reporters accompanying presidential trips and delaying publication until after trips ended; the restriction was controversial because it could be used arbitrarily to withhold information (e.g., private visits, possible health issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute secrecy for Manhattan Project and radar topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Manhattan Project and radar were treated as the two military topics that, if a code violation occurred, the office did not allow this to be used as a precedent for permitting other media outlets to report the same information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists were asked not to report on various phrases (e.g., "atom smashing", "atomic energy", "secret military weapons") and a list of element names was circulated (polonium, uranium, ytterbium, hafnium, protactinium, radium, rhenium, thorium, deuterium) to conceal uranium's special importance. The Office of Censorship was not told about the Manhattan Project until March 1943 and treated disclosures with extraordinary secrecy measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial measures for breaches and non-precedential handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When breaches occurred (e.g., the Mutual Network broadcast mentioning atom splitting), the Office of Censorship asked that all recordings of the broadcast be destroyed and stressed that such breaches not be treated as precedents for future reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office used strong remedial requests and insisted officials sometimes disclosed information without authorization; procedural errors that led to national-level disclosures prompted requests for destruction and damage control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media types and scope of monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office monitored overseas cables and telegrams (about 350,000 weekly), 25,000 international telephone calls per week, and maintained film review offices in Los Angeles, New York City, and Rochester, New York.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the scope and media-specific operations (telecommunications and film review) the Office used to identify and control sensitive information flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation and pledge system for correspondents
rubrics_metrics.description: All major news organizations in addition to 1,600 accredited wartime correspondents pledged to adhere to the Code of Wartime Practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accreditation and formal pledges were used as a mechanism to secure voluntary compliance and coordinate media behavior; a 24-hour hotline provided rapid guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle limiting censorship to war-related matters (avoid broader propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Price stated: "what does not concern the war does not concern censorship," and he opposed merging the Office of Censorship with the Office of War Information because he believed a merger would prevent the public from receiving truthful wartime information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle guided the Office to focus censorship strictly on operational security and avoid becoming a vehicle for political propaganda, distinguishing censorship from overt information/propaganda campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and institutional basis for wartime censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship authority rested on statutory and legal foundations such as the First War Powers Act (broad grants of Executive authority) and the Communications Act of 1934 (which made radio vulnerable); Attorney General Francis Biddle issued an opinion that gave the director nearly unlimited authority over broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These legal instruments and opinions provided the justification and scope for administrative censorship actions and coordination with military branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allied coordination and central clearinghouse of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives of Great Britain, Canada, and the United States signed an agreement providing for the complete exchange of information among all concerned parties and created a central clearinghouse of information within the headquarters of the Office of Censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International coordination aimed to harmonize censorship practices among Allies and to share intelligence about what constituted sensitive information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship failures highlight need for procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable failures (e.g., the Chicago Tribune's announcement about breaking the Japanese Purple cipher in June 1942; Congressman Andrew Jackson May's disclosure in 1943 about depth charges) exposed weaknesses that led to serious operational consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These incidents, and their consequences (e.g., estimated submarine losses), are presented as lessons underscoring the importance of strict procedures, oversight, and careful handling of classified or sensitive information.
